name: Backblaze Personal Backup
tagline: Continuously back up a selected computer to user-owned object storage and test restores

tiers.name: Computer Backup
tiers.limits: Unlimited backup data for 1 computer plus directly attached external drives; NAS devices are excluded.
tiers.notes: $99/year; a 2-year term is $189, equivalent to about $7.88/month.

pricing.billingTerms: monthly + annual + 2-year; subscriptions are priced per computer
pricing.hiddenCosts: 30-day version history is standard; 1-year history can be enabled without an added recurring fee, while Forever Version History bills data older than 1 year at $0.006/GB/month. Shipped USB restores require an upfront device charge, refundable only if returned within the stated window.

verdictSummary: A consolation build is possible, but the paid product's decisive value sits outside a solo rebuild. For Backblaze Personal Backup, continuously back up a selected computer to user-owned object storage and test restores. The hard boundary is unlimited backup economics, client reliability, restore logistics, support, and durable infrastructure, plus reliability, durability, and cross-device sync.
coreLoopDIY: Continuously back up selected folders, encrypt files client-side, track versions, restore them from user-owned object storage, and test restores regularly.
whatYouLose: unlimited backup economics, client reliability, restore logistics, support, and durable infrastructure
ongoingBurden: chunking, encryption, conflict detection, versions, garbage collection, bandwidth, restore drills, monitoring, billing, and disaster recovery
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Backblaze Personal Backup because storage subscriptions sell confidence that files will still exist after a lost device, bad sync, or provider incident. The recurring cost buys chunking, encryption, conflict detection, versions, garbage collection, bandwidth, restore drills, monitoring, billing, and disaster recovery, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Nextcloud
priorArt.desc: Mature open-source file sync and collaboration server.

alternatives.name: Backrest
alternatives.desc: Restic with buttons, schedules, checks, and enough guardrails to avoid living in a terminal.

facts.install: Standalone installer or Homebrew on macOS/Linux, Windows installer, or Docker Compose; it downloads/manages restic on first run
facts.dataFormat: Backups are encrypted, content-addressed restic repositories on the chosen local, SFTP, object-storage, or rclone target; Backrest keeps local JSON configuration, cache, and service data.
facts.gapVsPaid: It adds a friendly scheduler, but unlike Backblaze it includes no unlimited off-site storage, automatic destination, managed retention, or shipped physical restore.
facts.setupBlocker: You still have to choose and provision storage, protect the repository password, grant filesystem access, and test restores; macOS may require Full Disk Access.

alternatives.name: Duplicati
alternatives.desc: Browser-driven encrypted backups to nearly any storage target, with more knobs than charm.

facts.install: Signed Windows/macOS/Linux package or Docker container, then configure backups through its local web UI
facts.dataFormat: Each backup target contains encrypted compressed `.dblock` data volumes, `.dindex` indexes, and one `.dlist` manifest per version; a local database accelerates catalog and restore operations.
facts.gapVsPaid: It can automate encrypted backups, but you must choose and pay for storage, protect credentials, monitor jobs, and test restores yourself instead of getting Backblaze's managed service.
facts.setupBlocker: The first setup is not just an install: you must supply destination credentials, choose encryption and retention, preserve the passphrase, and understand how to rebuild from remote volumes if the local database is lost.

alternatives.name: Kopia
alternatives.desc: Encrypted snapshots to storage you choose; the cloud bill and restore drills are still yours.

facts.install: Install KopiaUI or the CLI from native Windows/macOS/Linux packages, then create or connect to a repository
facts.dataFormat: Snapshots live in an encrypted, deduplicated, content-addressed Kopia repository on local/NAS, SFTP, WebDAV, object storage, rclone, or supported cloud targets; small blocks are packed into opaque blobs.
facts.gapVsPaid: Its snapshots are excellent, but the storage account, capacity, billing, scheduling, monitoring, and restore drills are all your responsibility rather than Backblaze's.
facts.setupBlocker: You must provision and pay for the storage target, enter its credentials, and safeguard the repository password, Kopia cannot recover data if that password is lost.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Nextcloud Files
rejectedAlternatives.desc: File sync is not a tested backup system; deletions and bad changes can follow you.

rejectedAlternatives.name: restic
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Excellent backup engine; still a terminal, scheduler, and retention policy you must assemble yourself.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Computer Backup plan and a single-user encrypted backup DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a closest honest personal substitute for Backblaze Personal Backup in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, PostgreSQL, MinIO, and a Tauri 2 sync client; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: continuously back up selected folders, encrypt files client-side, track versions, restore them from user-owned object storage, and test restores regularly.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Build a desktop client that watches explicitly selected folders and ignores configured patterns.
Chunk, hash, compress, and encrypt files locally before uploading to the configured object store.
Store version metadata, tombstones, device identifiers, and integrity checks in PostgreSQL.
Provide upload and restore queues with pause, retry, bandwidth limits, and resumable transfers.
Add file history, point-in-time restore, key export, storage usage, and scheduled restore tests.
Document the failure model and make clear that one server is not a complete backup strategy.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Do not claim to reproduce proprietary data, network liquidity, regulated access, or frontier infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out multi-provider consumer sync at global scale.
Deliberately leave out guaranteed durability or ransomware recovery.
Deliberately leave out shared-drive administration, mobile apps, and enterprise compliance.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
